learn.heading: What is HTML?
paragraphs: HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It is the standard language used to create every webpage on the internet — from Google's homepage to your favourite social media feed.

Think of HTML as the skeleton of a webpage. Just like your skeleton gives your body its shape and structure, HTML gives a webpage its structure. Without it, the browser would have no idea what to display.

learn.heading: Tags — the building blocks
paragraphs:
HTML is made up of elements called tags. A tag is a keyword wrapped in angle brackets, like `

` or `

`.
Most tags come in pairs: an opening tag `<tagname>` and a closing tag `</tagname>` (note the forward slash). Your content goes between the two.

Some tags are self-closing — they do not need a closing tag. `` and `
` are the most common examples. You will meet those soon.

I am a paragraph.

I am a big heading

learn.heading: The DOCTYPE Declaration
paragraphs: Every HTML file must begin with exactly one line: `<!DOCTYPE html>`. This is not a tag — it is a declaration that tells the browser 'this document is HTML5'.
Without it, some browsers fall into 'quirks mode' and render your page in strange, unpredictable ways. Always include it as the very first line.

learn.heading: Further Reading
paragraphs: If you'd like a deeper reference, read the short textbook excerpt below before starting to code.

textbook.title: HTML5 Quick Reference
textbook.excerpt: MDN's HTML reference is a concise, authoritative guide to HTML elements and attributes.

learn.heading: Head and Body
paragraphs: After `<!DOCTYPE html>`, you wrap everything in an `<html>` element. Inside `<html>` there are exactly two children:
`<head>` — invisible metadata about the page: its title (shown in the browser tab), links to stylesheets, and scripts.
`<body>` — everything the user actually sees: text, images, buttons, forms. This is where you will spend most of your time.
Copy the snippet below into the editor to get started — then personalise the title!
learn.snippet:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>My Portfolio</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <!-- Your content goes here -->
  </body>
</html>

challenges.instructions: Build the full HTML skeleton: add `<!DOCTYPE html>`, then `<html>`, inside it `<head>` containing `<title>My Portfolio</title>`, and `<body>` tags.

learn.heading: Heading Elements
paragraphs: HTML provides six heading levels: `<h1>` through `<h6>`. `<h1>` is the largest and most important; `<h6>` is the smallest.
Headings are not just about size — they carry meaning. Screen readers and search engines use them to understand what a page is about. Always use one `<h1>` per page as the main title.

learn.heading: Using h1 for Your Name
paragraphs: On a portfolio page, your name is the most important piece of information — it is what recruiters, collaborators and clients see first.
Add an `<h1>` tag inside `<body>` with your name inside it. You can use any name you like for now and change it later.
Notice how the browser automatically makes `<h1>` large and bold — no CSS required yet. That is the browser's default stylesheet doing the work.

challenges.instructions: Inside the `<body>` tag, add an `<h1>` element containing your name.

learn.heading: Paragraphs in HTML
paragraphs:
Paragraphs are the most common way to add readable text to a webpage. The `

` tag wraps a block of text into a paragraph.

Browsers automatically add a small margin above and below each `

` element, giving your text breathing room. You do not need to add blank lines manually — HTML ignores extra whitespace in your source code.

learn.heading: Semantic HTML
paragraphs: HTML5 introduced 'semantic' elements — tags whose names describe their purpose. Instead of using `<div>` for everything, you use meaningful names like `<nav>`, `<header>`, `<section>`, and `<footer>`.

Semantic HTML is important for three reasons: it helps screen readers navigate for visually impaired users, it helps search engines understand your content, and it makes your code far easier to read and maintain.

learn.heading: The nav Element
paragraphs: The `<nav>` element wraps a group of navigation links. It signals to browsers, search engines, and assistive technologies: 'this area helps users move around the site'.
You can place `<nav>` inside `<header>` or directly in `<body>`. For now, add it after your intro paragraph.

learn.heading: Anchor Tags and href
paragraphs: Links in HTML use the `<a>` (anchor) tag. The destination is set with the `href` attribute — short for Hypertext REFerence.
To link to a section on the same page, use a `#` followed by the section's `id`, like `href="#about"`. When clicked, the browser jumps smoothly to that section.
The text between `` and `` is what the user sees and clicks.

challenges.instructions: Add a `<nav>` element inside `<body>`. Inside it, add two `<a>` links: one pointing to `#about` with text 'About', and one pointing to `#projects` with text 'Projects'.

challenges.title: About Me Section

learn.heading: Dividing Your Page into Sections
paragraphs: As pages grow, you need to divide content into logical regions. HTML5's `<section>` element groups related content together — like an 'About' area or a 'Projects' area.
Unlike a generic `<div>`, a `<section>` signals that its contents are thematically related. It should generally have a heading inside it.

learn.heading: The id Attribute
paragraphs: The `id` attribute gives an element a unique name on the page. No two elements should share the same `id`.

IDs are used for two things: navigating within a page (via `href="#id"`) and targeting elements with CSS or JavaScript. Remember your `<nav>` links point to `#about` and `#projects` — those IDs go on your `<section>` elements.
Add `id="about"` to your section tag: `<section id="about">`.

learn.heading: Organising Content with div
paragraphs: The `<div>` element is a generic container — it groups other elements together without adding any visual meaning. It's the most flexible building block in HTML.
Divs are useful for wrapping content you want to style together, like a project 'card': an image, a title, a description, and a link all inside one `<div>`.
learn.snippet:
My First Website

A portfolio built with HTML.

learn.heading: Heading Hierarchy
paragraphs: You already used `<h1>` for your name and `<h2>` for section titles. Inside a section, use `<h3>` for card-level titles.

Think of headings like a document outline: `<h1>` is the document title, `<h2>` are chapter names, `<h3>` are sub-topics within chapters. This hierarchy helps search engines index your content correctly.

challenges.instructions: Add a `<section id="projects">` after the About section. Inside it, add an `<h2>` with text 'Projects', then a `<div>` containing an `<h3>` with a project name of your choice.

learn.heading: Images in HTML
paragraphs: The `` tag embeds an image into a webpage. Unlike most HTML elements, `` is self-closing — it has no closing tag and no content between tags.
Every `` needs at least two attributes: `src` (the image source — a URL or file path) and `alt` (alternative text that describes the image for screen readers and shows if the image fails to load).

learn.heading: Attributes
paragraphs: Attributes add extra information to an HTML element. They always go inside the opening tag and follow the format `name="value"`.
You have already seen `id`, `href`, and now `src` and `alt`. HTML has dozens of attributes — you will pick them up naturally as you build more things.
The `alt` attribute is important for accessibility. Screen readers read it aloud to visually impaired users. Always write a meaningful description.

learn.heading: Hyperlinks — the Web's Superpower
paragraphs: The ability to link from one document to another is what makes the internet a 'web'. Every `<a>` tag is a hyperlink that connects pages together.
The `href` attribute sets the destination. It can be a full URL (`https://github.com`), a relative path (`/about`), or an anchor on the same page (`#projects`).

learn.heading: External Links
paragraphs: When linking to an external site, always include the full URL starting with `https://`. Without the protocol, the browser will treat it as a relative path and get lost.
Optionally, add `target="_blank"` to make the link open in a new browser tab — useful for external links so the user doesn't leave your portfolio.

challenges.instructions: Inside your projects `<div>`, after the `<h3>`, add an `<a>` tag with `href="https://github.com"` and the text 'View on GitHub'.

challenges.title: Contact Section
challenges.description: Let people reach you! Use a mailto link for a real-world touch.

learn.heading: The mailto Protocol
paragraphs: HTML links don't only go to web pages. The `mailto:` protocol opens the user's email client with the 'To' field already filled in.
It's one of the oldest and simplest ways to add contact functionality to a site — no server required.

learn.heading: Wrapping Up Your Portfolio
paragraphs: You now know enough HTML to build a real, structured webpage. Your portfolio has a navigation bar, sections, headings, a photo, links, and soon a contact section.

Add a final `<section id="contact">` after your projects section. Give it an `<h2>` heading and a `mailto:` link. Then you will have a complete first version of your portfolio — built entirely by hand!
